topic: Artillery, mortars, and heavy crew-served weapons in Russia-Ukraine war

findings.name: 2S19 Msta-S
findings.notes: Russia's primary self-propelled howitzer and backbone of Russian artillery in Ukraine. Russia had ~760 available at war start; 293+ visually confirmed losses by 2024. Ukraine captured many units and pressed them into service. Russia continuously pulls reserve stocks to replace losses and delivered new 2S19M2 variants to frontline units in 2023.

findings.name: BM-21 Grad
findings.notes: The single most numerically prevalent MLRS on both sides. Russia had ~1,000 active plus 2,000 in reserve at war start; Ukraine had ~185 active. Range 20-42 km. Used for area suppression fire. Both sides have documented extensive use. Russia also fields the modernized Tornado-G variant.

findings.name: M142 HIMARS
findings.designation: M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System
findings.notes: High strategic impact despite small numbers (~38 total delivered by US). Introduced June 2022; ~9,500 GMLRS rockets expended by Feb 2023. Reduced Russia's logistics advantage by striking supply depots deep behind lines. Effectiveness diminished by Russian electronic warfare/GPS jamming from 2023 onward. Fires GMLRS (70 km range) and ATACMS (300 km).

findings.name: M777 / M777A2
findings.notes: Most numerous Western towed howitzer supplied to Ukraine; ~152-198 delivered from USA, Canada, Australia. Prized for low weight (4,218 kg) and GPS-guided Excalibur rounds (40 km range). Over a third were damaged or destroyed by mid-2023 due to high fire rates burning out barrels. US established second barrel production line to meet demand.

findings.name: 2A65 Msta-B
findings.notes: Russia had 150 active + 600 in reserve; Ukraine had ~130 at war start. Russia lost 109 confirmed 2A65s in the first year; Ukraine lost 6. Both sides use this howitzer. Range 25-29 km standard, up to 29 km with RAP rounds. Fires all Soviet 152mm ammunition types. Cheaper and more plentiful than Western alternatives for both sides.

findings.name: 2S3 Akatsiya
findings.notes: Russia had ~500 active + 1,000 in reserve; Ukraine had ~249 at war start. Both sides use it extensively. Fires 43.56 kg HE-Frag shells to 18.5 km (standard) or longer with RAP. Considered a Cold War relic but still constitutes a huge portion of both armies' self-propelled artillery. Russia widely pulls these from storage as front-line losses mount.

findings.name: CAESAR
findings.notes: France delivered 18 initially plus additional units totaling ~30+ by 2024. Wheeled self-propelled howitzer on a 6x6 truck. Range 42-50 km. Praised for high mobility (shoot-and-scoot capability) and long range. Used effectively in the 2022 Kherson offensive. Ukraine received older 6x6 and newer 8x8 variants.

findings.name: PzH 2000
findings.notes: Germany and Netherlands jointly supplied ~14-18 units; Italy also contributed several. Tracked self-propelled howitzer with 67 km range using V-LAP and up to 47 km with standard rounds. High rate of fire (8 rpm burst). Considered one of the most capable western SPH in Ukrainian use. Maintenance-intensive; crews trained in Germany.

findings.name: AHS Krab
findings.notes: Poland delivered ~18 AHS Krab in 2022 with additional batches ordered. Tracked self-propelled howitzer with 30 km range (standard) up to 40 km with extended rounds. Uses NATO-standard 155mm ammunition. Saw notable use in the 2022 Kherson offensive and Bakhmut fighting.

findings.name: Archer FH77BW L52
findings.designation: Archer Artillery System / Artillerisystem 08 / FH77BW L52
findings.notes: Sweden transferred 8 Archer systems to Ukraine in January 2023 (later expanded to 26 total per 2025 reports). Fully automated wheeled SPH with 52-caliber barrel; range up to 60 km. Unique shoot-and-scoot capability allowing it to fire and relocate in seconds. Ukraine praised its survivability and precision in Donetsk combat operations.

findings.name: AS-90
findings.notes: UK donated 20 battle-ready AS-90s plus 12 non-functional spares in 2023; first combat use June 2023. Tracked SPH with 155mm L31 gun. Ukrainian forces reported it outperformed Soviet-era artillery systems they had used previously. UK withdrew them from their own inventory to supply Ukraine.

findings.name: 2S22 Bohdana
findings.notes: Ukraine's domestically produced wheeled SPH. By late 2024, Ukraine produced 150+ units and reached 40/month production rate. As of 2025 accounts for ~40% of all Ukrainian artillery on the frontline. Used the Snake Island shelling mission in June 2022 in its combat debut. Fires NATO 155mm standard ammunition.

findings.name: M109 (multiple variants)
findings.notes: ~90 M109 systems of various marks operated by Ukraine as of early 2024, supplied by Norway (M109A3GN), Belgium (M109A4), Italy, Latvia and the US (M109A6 Paladin). Used in multiple brigades. A widely dispersed and workhorse system within Ukraine's Western artillery fleet.

findings.name: M270 MLRS / MARS II
findings.designation: M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System / MARS II
findings.notes: UK supplied initial M270s from June 2022 (6 total); Germany supplied MARS II (German variant); by April 2023 Ukraine had at least 10 platforms from allied nations. Tracked launcher fires same GMLRS rockets as HIMARS but carries 12 rockets vs HIMARS's 6. No confirmed losses in public reports as of mid-2023.

findings.name: BM-27 Uragan
findings.notes: Russia had ~200 active; Ukraine had ~70 at war start. Range 35 km with 16-tube launcher. Used in several high-profile attacks on civilian infrastructure. Fires a wide variety of warheads including cluster munitions and incendiary rockets. The Chasiv Yar apartment block strike in July 2022 killing 48+ was attributed to a Uragan.

findings.name: BM-30 Smerch / Tornado-S
findings.notes: Russia had 100+ Smerch active in 2022 plus the modernized Tornado-S which fires guided rockets to 120 km. Ukraine also operated ~50 Smerch units. Russia deployed Tornado-S in Ukraine from February 2022. Range 70-90 km for Smerch; up to 120 km for Tornado-S guided rockets. Used in the Kharkiv shelling campaign.

findings.name: D-30
findings.notes: Russia had ~150 active + 4,400 in reserve; Ukraine had ~100 active at war start but Russia lost 76 confirmed D-30s in first year. Light, versatile howitzer with 360-degree traverse. Range 15.3 km standard. Used by both sides for direct and indirect fire support. Extremely common Soviet-era gun that is cheap, reliable, and plentiful.

findings.name: 2A36 Giatsint-B
findings.notes: Ukraine had ~180 at war start. Used by both Russia and Ukraine in the Donbas fighting since 2014. Long-range (26.5-33.5 km) towed field gun. Finland also supplied Ukraine with 152 K-89 guns (Finnish versions of this system). Russia used them in the Donbas before shifting to self-propelled platforms for survivability.

findings.name: 2S7 Pion / 2S7M Malka
findings.notes: Russia had ~50 active + 260 in reserve; Ukraine had 13 active + 83 stored, and returned the Pion to active service in 2022. Extremely powerful 203mm gun capable of firing nuclear shells in theory. Range 37.5-47.5 km. In June 2023 Ukraine started using American M106 203mm shells (from M110 howitzer stocks) in their Pion guns. Russia deployed the modernized 2S7M Malka variant in Ukraine.

findings.name: 2S5 Giatsint-S
findings.notes: Ukraine had 18 at war start; Russia had fewer than 500 active. Long-range SPG (15-29 km with standard rounds, up to 33.5 km with RAP). Used by both Ukrainian and Russian armies in the Donbas since 2014 and in the 2022 full-scale invasion.

findings.name: 2S1 Gvozdika
findings.notes: Ukraine had ~292 active; Russia had ~500 active + 1,800 in reserve. Light tracked SPH. Range 15.2 km standard. Used extensively by both sides due to sheer quantity available from Soviet stockpiles. Czech Republic also supplied RM-70 and Dana systems complementing Ukraine's Soviet-caliber fleet.

findings.name: 2B11 / 2S12 Sani
findings.notes: Standard heavy mortar of both armies. Ukraine had ~190 Sani systems and 30 PM-38 at war start. The 2B11 is the mortar barrel weighing ~210 kg, mounted on a wheeled 2L81 carriage forming the 2S12 Sani system. Range approximately 7.1 km. Towed by GAZ-66 truck. Ubiquitous at battalion level across both armies.

findings.name: M120-15 Molot
findings.notes: Ukrainian-developed 120mm mortar built at Kyiv plant Mayak. Developed from the Soviet 2B11 design in two months at the start of the Donbas war. Mass 230 kg. Ukraine had 120 units pre-war and continued producing them. Fires all Soviet-compatible 120mm ammunition. Part of Ukraine's effort to maintain mortar capability with domestic production.

findings.name: 2B14 Podnos
findings.notes: Standard Soviet-designed light mortar used by both armies for infantry-level fire support. Designed in the early 1980s as a replacement for the WWII-era BM-37. Man-portable for airborne and light infantry units. Smoothbore design. Range approximately 4 km. Both Ukrainian and Russian forces rely on this as the standard company/battalion mortar.

findings.name: PM-38 / M1938
findings.notes: WWII-era Soviet heavy mortar still in service with both armies due to massive stockpile quantities. Ukraine had 30 at war start. Derived from a French Brandt design produced under license. Compatible with 120mm ammunition used by 2B11 and modern mortars. Often captured and reused by both sides.

findings.name: DShK / DShKM
findings.notes: WWII-era Soviet heavy machine gun still in widespread use. Ukraine modified DShKs with NSV muzzle brakes, bipods, and shoulder stocks as infantry anti-materiel weapons during the 2014 Donbas war, continuing into 2022. Used as anti-personnel, anti-light-vehicle, and anti-drone weapon. Both sides use vehicle-mounted variants extensively. Known as 'Dushka' (Little Soul) among troops.

findings.name: NSV / NSVS
findings.notes: Replaced DShK in Soviet service from 1971. Used on vehicle pintle mounts and tripod by both Russian and Ukrainian forces. Both sides have inherited stocks from Soviet dissolution. Poland produces a copy (NSW) and various former Soviet states operate the platform. Can be distinguished from the Kord by external features - often misidentified in field reports.

findings.name: Kord (6P50 / 6P57)
findings.notes: Modern Russian replacement for the NSV, entering service 1998. Mounted on most modern Russian tanks (T-80U, T-90). Infantry version uses 6T19 bipod or 6T7 tripod. Low recoil design allows firing from a bipod unlike heavier predecessors. Russia created assault companies in Ukraine using Kord as primary heavy direct-fire weapon in manpower-saving tactics. Also used by Wagner Group units.

findings.name: AGS-17 Plamya
findings.notes: Standard automatic grenade launcher of both armies. Operated from a tripod or vehicle/installation mount. Fires 30mm VOG-17M HE grenades at 350-400 rpm from 29-round belts. Effective range 1.7 km; designed to engage targets in trenches and behind terrain folds. Both Russian and Ukrainian territorial defense forces are documented using it. Russia's airborne forces use it extensively in Ukraine. Ukraine developed a miniaturized handheld variant (RGSh-30).

findings.name: Fort-500 Series
findings.notes: Ukrainian-manufactured pump-action shotgun based on the Remington 870 mechanism. Produced by RPC Fort. Variants include fixed wooden stock (500), folding stock (500A), and retractable CAA CBS stock (500T). Capacity 4 or 6 rounds. Used by Ukrainian forces in trench-level counter-drone defense. Part of Ukraine MoD's authorized pump-action shotgun modernization program. The 500T model is frequently documented in military use due to its compact profile.

findings.name: Hatsan Escort BTS 12
findings.notes: Turkish-made semi-automatic shotgun adopted by at least the 68th Jaeger Brigade of the Ukrainian army for anti-drone operations. Reported in 2024 as part of Ukraine's effort to equip infantry with shotguns for counter-UAV close-range defense against small FPV drones attacking trench positions.

findings.name: Hima Arms Safari HG-105M
findings.designation: Hima Arms Safari HG-105M Semi-Automatic Shotgun
findings.notes: Bullpup semi-automatic shotgun acquired by Ukraine from October 2024 for counter-drone use. Full-length barrel in a compact overall package due to bullpup layout. Specifically selected to engage small FPV and aerial UAVs at close range near trench lines. Part of Ukraine's documented program of equipping infantry with shotguns as drone defense tools.

findings.name: Zuzana 2
findings.notes: Slovak wheeled self-propelled howitzer supplied to Ukraine starting in 2022. At least 8-16 units delivered. 155mm NATO-standard system with 40 km range. Wheelbase provides good mobility. Slovakia also supplied the older Zuzana (152mm) and DANA SPH. Delivered as part of Slovakia's substantial military aid package.

Pages fetched from armyrecognition.com, nationalsecurityjournal.org, en.defence-ua.com, armyrecognition.com analysis pages, and multiple Wikipedia articles.
